column2: Also on the authority of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: “While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one day, there appeared before us a man whose clothes were exceedingly white and whose hair was exceedingly black.

No trace of travel could be seen on him, and none of us knew him. He came and sat down by the Prophet ﷺ, rested his knees against his knees, placed his palms on his thighs, and said: O Muḥammad, tell me about Islam.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer,

give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it. He said: You have spoken truly. We were amazed at him: he asks him and then confirms him! He said: Then tell me about faith (īmān).

He said: That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and that you believe in the decree (qadar), its good and its bad. He said: You have spoken truly. Then tell me about excellence (iḥsān).
He said: That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and though you do not see Him, He surely sees you. He said: Then tell me about the Hour.
He said: The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking. He said: Then tell me about its signs.

He said: That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings. Then he left, and I stayed a long while. Then he said: O ʿUmar, do you know who the questioner was?
I said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: That was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” Reported by Muslim.

This hadith of Jibrīl from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) was recorded by Muslim alone, without al-Bukhārī, while both of them recorded it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him). Imam al-Nawawī (may Allah have mercy on him) began the Forty with the hadith of ʿUmar, “Actions are only by intentions”,
which is the first hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, and placed second the hadith of ʿUmar telling of Jibrīl's coming to the Prophet ﷺ,
which is the first hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. Imam al-Baghawī preceded him in this in his two books Sharḥ al-Sunnah and Maṣābīḥ al-Sunnah, for he opened both of them with these two hadiths.
I have devoted a separate commentary to this hadith, more extensive than the explanation given here.
This hadith is the first hadith in the Book of Faith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar narrated it from his father,

and there is a story behind his narrating it, which Muslim mentions before this hadith with his chain from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, who said: “The first to speak about the decree (qadar) in al-Baṣrah was Maʿbad al-Juhanī. Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥimyarī and I set out for Ḥajj or ʿUmrah,

and we said: If only we could meet one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ask him about what these people say regarding the decree. Then we happened upon ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb as he was entering the mosque,
and my companion and I flanked him, one of us on his right and the other on his left. I thought my companion would leave the talking to me, so I said: O Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān,

there have appeared in our parts people who recite the Qurʾān and seek out knowledge—and he described their affairs—and they claim that there is no decree and that the matter is new (not foreordained). He said: When you meet those people, tell them that I am free of them and they are free of me. By the One by whom ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar swears,
if one of them had gold equal to Mount Uḥud and spent it, Allah would not accept it from him until he believes in the decree. Then he said: My father, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, narrated to me…”,
and he related the hadith in order to use it as evidence for belief in the decree. This story shows that the innovation of the Qadariyyah appeared in the time of the Companions,

during the lifetime of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), who died in the year 73 AH; that the Successors used to refer to the Companions of the Messenger ﷺ to learn the matters of the religion, and this is what is obligatory, namely to refer to the people of knowledge at all times,
because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know” [al-Naḥl 16:43]; that the innovation of the Qadariyyah is one of the most repugnant innovations,
given the severity of what Ibn ʿUmar said about it; and that when a muftī states a ruling, he should mention its evidence along with it.
The hadith of Jibrīl is evidence that the angels come to human beings in human form. Likewise, the Qurʾān tells of Jibrīl's coming to Maryam in the form of a man,
and the angels' coming to Ibrāhīm and Lūṭ in human form. By the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, they change from the form in which they were created into human form.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says concerning the creation of the angels: “All praise is due to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers having wings, two, three and four. He increases in creation what He wills” [Fāṭir 35:1].
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4857) and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (280) it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibrīl with six hundred wings.
In Jibrīl's coming to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his sitting before him there is an illustration of some of the etiquette of students of knowledge in the presence of the teacher;

and it shows that the questioner should not confine his questions to matters whose ruling he does not know; he should also ask about things whose ruling he knows, so that those present may hear the answer.

That is why the Messenger ﷺ attributed the teaching to him at the end of the hadith, saying: “That was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” The teaching came from the Prophet ﷺ, since he was the one who directly gave it, and it is attributed to Jibrīl
because he was its cause.
His words: “He said: O Muḥammad, tell me about Islam.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer,
give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.” When Jibrīl asked him about Islam, the Prophet ﷺ answered with outward matters,

and when he asked him about faith, he answered with inward matters. The words islām and īmān are among those which, when mentioned together, differ in meaning. Here they are mentioned together, so Islam is explained by outward matters, which suit the meaning of islām,

namely submission and yielding to Allah the Exalted, and faith is explained by inward matters, which suit its meaning, namely affirmation and acknowledgement. When either is mentioned on its own, it covers both meanings together: the outward and the inward matters. An example of islām mentioned on its own is the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers” [Āl ʿImrān 3:85]. An example of īmān mentioned on its own is the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:

“Whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have come to nothing, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers” [al-Māʾidah 5:5]. Comparable to this are the words faqīr and miskīn (poor and needy), birr and taqwā (righteousness and piety), and others.

The first of the matters by which Islam is explained is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. These two testimonies are inseparable from each other,
and they are binding on every human and jinn from the time he ﷺ was sent until the Hour is established. Whoever does not believe in him ﷺ is among the people of the Fire,
because he ﷺ said: “By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad,
no one of this nation, Jew or Christian, hears of me and then dies without believing in what I was sent with, except that he will be among the people of the Fire.” Reported by Muslim (240).

The testimony that there is no god but Allah means: there is no one rightfully worshipped except Allah. This statement of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlāṣ) comprises two pillars: a general negation at its beginning and a specific affirmation at its end.

At its beginning is the negation of worship from everyone other than Allah, and at its end the affirmation of worship for Allah alone, without partner. The predicate of the lā that negates the whole genus is understood to be “rightfully” (ḥaqq); it is not valid to understand it as “existing” (mawjūd),
because false gods do exist and are many. What is negated is only rightful divinity, which is negated from everyone other than Allah and established for Allah alone.

The meaning of the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah is that he is loved more than anyone else in creation is loved, that he is obeyed in everything he commands and that one refrains from everything he forbids,

that all his reports are believed, whether about the past, the future or the present, even though they are unseen and unwitnessed, and that Allah is worshipped in accordance with the truth and guidance he brought.
Devoting deeds sincerely to Allah and following what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ brought are what the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah requires.
Every deed by which one seeks nearness to Allah must be done sincerely for Allah and in conformity with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. If sincerity is missing, the deed is not accepted,
because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “And We will turn to whatever deeds they did and make them scattered dust” [al-Furqān 25:23], and because He, the Exalted, says in the ḥadīth qudsī:

“Of all partners, I am the most free of need of partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates someone else with Me, I abandon him and his association.” Reported by Muslim (2985). If following the Sunnah is missing, the deed is rejected,

because he ﷺ said: “Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (2697) and Muslim (1718). In a wording of Muslim: “Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected.” This wording is more general than the first,
because it includes both the one who does the innovation as its originator and the one who does it following someone else in it.
Some of what relates to prayer, zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj will be touched upon in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, “Islam is built upon five”, which is the hadith that follows this one.
His words: “He said: You have spoken truly. We were amazed at him: he asks him and then confirms him!

” The reason for their amazement is that a questioner usually does not know the answer and asks in order to arrive at it, and such a person does not say to the one he asked, after he answers: You have spoken truly,
because when the questioner confirms the one asked, it shows that he already had an answer. That is why the Companions were amazed at this confirmation from this stranger who was asking.
His words: “He said: Then tell me about faith.
He said: That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and that you believe in the decree, its good and its bad.” This answer comprises the six pillars of faith.
The first of these pillars is belief in Allah, which is the foundation for believing in everything that must be believed in. That is why the angels, the books and the messengers are spoken of as His.

Whoever does not believe in Allah does not believe in the rest of the pillars. Belief in Allah includes belief in His existence, His lordship, His divinity, and His names and attributes, and that He, Glorified and Exalted is He, is described by every perfection befitting Him and is free of every deficiency. It is therefore obligatory to affirm His oneness in His lordship, His divinity, and His names and attributes.

Affirming His oneness in His lordship is acknowledging that He is one in His actions and has no partner in them, such as creating, providing, giving life, causing death, directing affairs, disposing of the universe, and other matters related to His lordship.

Oneness of divinity is affirming His oneness through the actions of His servants, such as supplication, fear, hope, reliance, seeking help, seeking refuge, calling for rescue, sacrifice, vows and other kinds of worship that must be devoted to Him alone. None of it may be directed to anyone other than Him, even if it were an angel brought near or a prophet sent as a messenger, let alone anyone else.

As for the oneness of the names and attributes, it is affirming all the names and attributes that He affirmed for Himself and that His Messenger ﷺ affirmed for Him, in a manner befitting His perfection and majesty,

without asking how (takyīf) or likening (tamthīl), and without distorting (taḥrīf), reinterpreting (taʾwīl) or negating (taʿṭīl); and declaring Him free of everything that does not befit Him, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing” [al-Shūrā 42:11]. In this verse He combined affirmation with declaring Him free of imperfection: the affirmation is in His words, “and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing,” and the declaration of His freedom from imperfection in His words,

“There is nothing like unto Him.” So He, Glorified and Exalted is He, has hearing unlike any hearing and sight unlike any sight, and the same is said of every name and attribute established for Allah.

Belief in the angels is believing that they are among the creatures of Allah, created from light, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2996), where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire,

and Ādam was created from what has been described to you.” They have wings, as in the first verse of Sūrat Fāṭir, and Jibrīl has six hundred wings, as is established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and was mentioned just above.

They are a vast creation whose number none knows except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Evidence of this is that the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr), which is in the seventh heaven, is entered every day by seventy thousand angels who never return to it. Reported by al-Bukhārī (3207) and Muslim (259).

Muslim also reported in his Ṣaḥīḥ (2842) from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Hell will be brought forth on that Day with seventy thousand reins, and with each rein seventy thousand angels pulling it.”

Among the angels are those entrusted with revelation, those entrusted with rain, those entrusted with death, those entrusted with wombs, those entrusted with Paradise, those entrusted with the Fire, and those entrusted with other things. All of them submit and comply with the command of Allah: they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.

Among those named in the Book and the Sunnah are Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl, Mālik, Munkar and Nakīr. It is obligatory to believe in those of them who are named and those who are not named, and it is also obligatory to believe in and affirm every report about the angels in the Mighty Book or authentically established in the Sunnah.

Belief in the books is affirming and acknowledging every book that Allah sent down to one of His messengers, and believing that they are true, that they are revealed and not created, that they contain what brings happiness to those to whom they were sent down, and that whoever holds to them is safe and successful,

while whoever turns away from them fails and loses. Some of these books are named in the Qurʾān and some are not. Those named in the Qurʾān are the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scriptures of Ibrāhīm and Mūsā. The scriptures of Ibrāhīm and Mūsā are mentioned in two places in the Qurʾān,

in Sūrat al-Najm and Sūrat al-Aʿlā. The Psalms of Dāwūd are mentioned in the Qurʾān in two places, in al-Nisāʾ and al-Isrāʾ, where Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says in both: “And to Dāwūd We gave the Psalms” [al-Nisāʾ 4:163; al-Isrāʾ 17:55]. As for the Torah and the Gospel, they are mentioned in many sūrahs of the Qurʾān,

and the more frequently mentioned of the two is the Torah. No messenger is mentioned in the Qurʾān as often as Mūsā, and no book is mentioned in it as often as the book of Mūsā, which is referred to as “the Torah”, “the Book”, “the Criterion”, “the Light” and “the Reminder”.

Among the features that distinguish the Qurʾān from the earlier books are that it is the everlasting miracle, that Allah has undertaken to preserve it, that it is safe from distortion, and that it was revealed in stages, piece by piece.
Belief in the messengers is affirming and acknowledging that Allah chose from among humankind messengers and prophets who guide people to the truth and bring them out of darkness into light.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind” [al-Ḥajj 22:75]. There are no messengers among the jinn, but there are warners among them, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“And when We directed to you a group of the jinn, listening to the Qurʾān; when they attended it, they said: Listen quietly. And when it was concluded, they went back to their people as warners. They said: O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Mūsā, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path. O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment. And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape [Him] on earth, and he will have no protectors besides Him. Those are in clear error” [al-Aḥqāf 46:29–32].

They did not mention any messengers from among themselves, nor any books revealed to them; they mentioned only the two books revealed to Mūsā and Muḥammad (blessings and peace be upon them both). The Gospel was not mentioned even though it was revealed after Mūsā,
because many of the rulings in the Gospel had already come in the Torah. Ibn Kathīr said in his tafsīr of these verses: “They did not mention ʿĪsā,

because the Gospel was revealed to ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) containing admonitions, words that soften the heart, and a little on what is lawful and unlawful; in reality it is like a completion of the law of the Torah, so the principal reference is the Torah. That is why they said: ‘revealed after Mūsā’.”

The messengers are those charged with conveying laws revealed to them, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “We have already sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the Balance” [al-Ḥadīd 57:25], “the Book” being a generic noun meaning the books.
The prophets are those to whom it was revealed that they should convey an earlier law, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged for the Jews, as did the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah” [al-Māʾidah 5:44], to the end of the verse.

The messengers and prophets conveyed what they were commanded to convey completely and perfectly, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Is there anything upon the messengers except clear conveyance?” [al-Naḥl 16:35]

and He said: “Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates are opened and its keepers say to them: Did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours? They will say: Yes, indeed; but the word of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers” [al-Zumar 39:71]. Al-Zuhrī said: “From Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, comes the message;
upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is the conveying; and upon us is submission.” Al-Bukhārī cited it in his Ṣaḥīḥ, in the Book of Tawḥīd, in the chapter on the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:
“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message” [al-Māʾidah 5:67] (13/503, with Fatḥ al-Bārī).

Among the messengers are those whose stories are told in the Qurʾān and those whose stories are not told, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And messengers We have told you about before, and messengers We have not told you about” [al-Nisāʾ 4:164]. And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“We have already sent messengers before you; among them are those whose stories We have told you and among them are those whose stories We have not told you” [Ghāfir 40:78]. Those whose stories are told in the Qurʾān are twenty-five, eighteen of whom are mentioned in Sūrat al-Anʿām, in the saying of the Exalted:

“And that was Our argument which We gave Ibrāhīm against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will; indeed, your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing. And We gave him Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, each of whom We guided; and Nūḥ We guided before; and among his descendants, Dāwūd, Sulaymān, Ayyūb, Yūsuf, Mūsā and Hārūn. Thus do We reward those who do good. And Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā, ʿĪsā and Ilyās, each of them among the righteous; and Ismāʿīl, al-Yasaʿ, Yūnus and Lūṭ, and each of them We favoured above the worlds” [al-Anʿām 6:83–86].
The remaining seven are Ādam, Idrīs, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, Dhū al-Kifl and Muḥammad, may the blessings, peace and grace of Allah be upon them all.
Belief in the Last Day is affirming and acknowledging everything the Book and the Sunnah tell us about all that will happen after death. Allah has made two abodes:
the abode of this world and the abode of the Hereafter. The boundary separating these two abodes is death and the blowing of the Trumpet, by which those still alive at the end of this world will die.

When anyone dies, his own resurrection has begun, and he has moved from the abode of deeds to the abode of recompense. Life after death is of two kinds: the life of the barzakh, which is between death and the resurrection, and the life after death [that follows the resurrection]. None knows the reality of the life of the barzakh except Allah, and it is connected with the life after death,

because in each of them there is recompense for deeds: the people of happiness enjoy in their graves the bliss of Paradise, and the people of misery are punished in them with the punishment of the Fire.

Included in belief in the Last Day is belief in the resurrection, the gathering, the intercession, the Basin, the reckoning, the Balance, the Bridge, Paradise, the Fire and everything else mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah.
Belief in the decree is believing that Allah has decreed everything that will be until the Day of Resurrection. It has four levels:
Allah's knowledge from eternity of everything that will be;
His writing of the measures [of all things] fifty thousand years before creating the heavens and the earth;
His willing of everything decreed;
and Allah's creating and bringing into being everything He decreed, in accordance with what He knew, wrote and willed.
It is obligatory to believe in these levels and to believe that everything Allah wills must come to be, and that nothing Allah has not willed can possibly come to be.
This is the meaning of what he ﷺ said: “And know that what has befallen you was not going to miss you, and what has missed you was not going to befall you,” which will come in the nineteenth hadith.
His words: “Then tell me about excellence.

He said: That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and though you do not see Him, He surely sees you.” Excellence (iḥsān) is the highest level; below it is the level of faith, and below that the level of Islam. Every believer is a Muslim,

and everyone who has excellence (a muḥsin) is a believer and a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer and a muḥsin. That is why it says in Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt: “The Bedouins say: We have believed. Say: You have not believed; but say: We have submitted (aslamnā), for faith has not yet entered your hearts” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:14].

In this hadith the loftiness of the level of excellence is made clear in his words: “That you worship Allah as though you see Him”, meaning that you worship Him as though you are standing before Him, seeing Him. Whoever is like this performs worship completely and perfectly.

If he is not in this state, he should be mindful that Allah is watching him and that nothing of him is hidden from Him, so that he is wary of Allah seeing him where He has forbidden him to be, and strives to be seen by Him where He has commanded him to be.
His words: “He said: Then tell me about the Hour.

He said: The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking.” Allah has reserved knowledge of the Hour for Himself; none knows when the Hour will be established except Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

“Indeed, with Allah is knowledge of the Hour. He sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware” [Luqmān 31:34].

And the Exalted said: “With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He” [al-Anʿām 6:59], and among them is knowledge of the Hour. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4778) it is reported that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said:
The Prophet ﷺ said: “The keys of the unseen are five,” and then he recited: “Indeed, with Allah is knowledge of the Hour.” And the Exalted said:

“They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him. It lies heavy upon the heavens and the earth; it will not come to you except suddenly. They ask you as if you were well informed about it. Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah, but most people do not know” [al-Aʿrāf 7:187]. The Sunnah tells us that the Hour will be established on a Friday. But in which year?
In which month of the year?
On which Friday of the month?
None knows that except Allah. In Sunan Abī Dāwūd (1046) it is reported that Abū Hurayrah said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The best day on which the sun has risen is Friday.

On it Ādam was created, on it he was sent down [to earth], on it his repentance was accepted, on it he died, and on it the Hour will be established. There is no creature that is not listening attentively on Friday from dawn until the sun rises,

in fear of the Hour, except the jinn and mankind…”, to the end of the hadith. It is an authentic hadith whose narrators are narrators of the six books, except al-Qaʿnabī, from whom Ibn Mājah did not narrate.

His words, “The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking,” mean that created beings do not know when it will be established, and that anyone asking and anyone asked are alike in not knowing it.
His words: “He said: Then tell me about its signs.

He said: That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings.” Amārātuhā means its signs. The signs of the Hour are of two kinds: signs close to its establishment,

such as the rising of the sun from the west, the emergence of the Dajjāl, the emergence of Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj, the descent of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (blessings and peace be upon him) from the sky, and others; and signs before that, among which are the two signs mentioned in this hadith.

The meaning of his words, “That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress,” has been explained as an indication of many conquests and many captives: some of the captive women would be taken by their masters and bear them children,

so she becomes an umm walad, and her child has the standing of her master. It has also been explained as a change in conditions, with children becoming undutiful to their fathers and mothers and domineering over them, until the children are as though they were masters of their fathers and mothers.

The meaning of his words, “and that you see the barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings,” is that the poor who herd sheep and cannot find anything to clothe themselves with will have their conditions change: they will move to live in the cities and compete with one another there in raising tall buildings. Both of these signs have already come to pass.
His words: “Then he left, and I stayed a long while. Then he said: O ʿUmar, do you know who the questioner was?

I said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: That was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” Maliyyan means “for a while”. The Prophet ﷺ informed his Companions that the questioner was Jibrīl right after he left, while it is also reported that he informed ʿUmar after three [nights]. There is no contradiction between these,

because the Prophet ﷺ informed those present while ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) was not with them, having left the gathering; it then happened that he met the Prophet ﷺ after three [nights], and he informed him.
A questioner may ask in order to teach, just as he asks in order to learn: he asks someone who has knowledge of something so that those present may hear the answer.
The angels change from the form in which they were created and come in the shapes of human beings. This is no evidence for the permissibility of the acting that has become widespread in these times,
for it is a kind of lying, while what happened with Jibrīl was by the permission and power of Allah.
The hadith shows the etiquette of a learner in the presence of the teacher.
When islām and īmān are mentioned together, islām is explained by outward matters and īmān by inward matters.
One should begin with what is most important, then with what is next in importance,
since the explanation of Islam began with the two testimonies, and the explanation of faith began with belief in Allah.
The pillars of Islam are five, and the foundations of faith are six.
Belief in the six foundations of faith is part of belief in the unseen.
Islam, faith and excellence differ in degree.
The hadith shows how lofty the level of excellence is.
Knowledge of the Hour is among the things Allah has kept to Himself.
The hadith mentions some of the signs of the Hour.
One who is asked about something he does not know should say: Allah knows best.
